name: streaming-processing
context: An unbounded sequence of events must be transformed continuously, one record at a time, with results visible in milliseconds rather than at the end of a batch window. The defining mechanics are incremental computation over a partitioned, replayable log; parallelism bounded by partition count; ordering guaranteed only per key; local state for anything that needs memory; and event time as the only clock that survives restarts and replays. This is the base style, not a specific data-lake decision — it applies to transaction processing, telemetry, IoT and clickstream alike.
benefits: Results appear within milliseconds of the triggering record instead of at the next batch boundary
Replayability is inherent: the log is the input, so logic can be re-executed over history without special tooling
Scaling is horizontal and bounded by partition count, with per-key ordering preserved automatically
Exactly-once is achievable where the framework is tightly integrated with the log — offsets, state and output commit atomically
Graceful degradation is natural: a downstream that is down creates lag, not data loss
tradeoffs: Exactly-once requires end-to-end integration with the log; a framework that treats the broker as an external system cannot deliver it, and generic sinks do not participate
Out-of-order data is the normal case, not the exception — stream-stream joins handle it, table joins often do not
Long-running stateful processes need restart, restore and rebalance machinery that batch jobs do not
Failure semantics are constant: a task restart replays from the last commit, so state and time advance together
No full recomputation for free — a logic change means either replaying history or accepting divergence between old and new results
use_cases: Real-time transaction authorization and fraud scoring over a payment event log
IoT telemetry ingestion with per-device aggregation published as it arrives
Clickstream analytics with incremental sessionization and funnel metrics
Continuous operational monitoring: alerting on stream predicates rather than on stored queries
Order and inventory workflows where business decisions depend on events happening now
avoid_when: The workload is inherently bounded and complete results are needed before any output is useful
The team has no operational capability for long-running processes, restarts and replay
Strong cross-key consistency is a hard requirement and there is no reconciling store downstream
Batch is already fast enough and the added failure modes buy nothing
component_types: Partitioned log: ordered, replayable record stream supplying both input and parallelism
Source processor: reads a partition and drives per-task processing
Stateless operator: per-record transformation with no memory
Stateful operator: aggregation, join or window backed by a local store
Changelog and commit protocol: durability for state plus atomic offset and output commit
Sink processor: writes results back to the log or to an external transactional sink
anti_patterns: Claiming exactly-once because the broker is transactional, when the sink does not participate in the transaction
Using processing-time windows over event-time data and calling the result late-arrival-safe
Scaling consumers past the partition count and believing the extra capacity is used
Treating a state store's local cache as the source of truth rather than the changelog
Running a long batch-style computation inside a streaming job simply because the input happens to be a log
design_principles: One record at a time: incremental computation over an unbounded input
The log is the input, the state and the recovery mechanism
Parallelism is bounded by partitions; per-key order is the only order guaranteed
Event time is the clock; wall clock is a performance detail
Failure is a rewind, not a stop
best_practices: Decide explicitly between at-least-once and exactly-once per output, and document which sinks qualify
Size partitions to the parallelism you intend to reach, then treat it as a hard ceiling
Design for out-of-order arrival from the first version, including late-arrival handling for every windowed result
Test by killing tasks mid-stream, not by running the happy path
Replay-based recovery requires idempotent sinks unless the sink participates in the transaction
references: Apache Kafka, Core Concepts — processor topologies, event vs processing vs ingestion time, processing guarantees, https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/core-concepts/
Apache Flink, Timely Stream Processing — event time, watermarks and lateness, https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-master/docs/concepts/time/
Apache Flink, Windows — window assigners, triggers and allowed lateness, https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/operators/windows/
Apache Kafka, Streams Architecture — tasks, partitions and fault tolerance, https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/architecture/
